These patterns and course are based on long-time machine knitter and knitwear designer Jodi Raymond's series of printed "Upside Down Raglan" books.
  • They've been updated and the "text-heavy" instructions have been re-written for easier reading.
  • The written instructions are now in a step-by-step checklist format.
  • The diagrams have been re-formatted making them easier to follow
  • Also included are links to relevant videos and additional instruction for each step of the way.
  • Copyright
    FYI, Knit it Now purchased the rights to Jodi's books a few years ago. There is no copyright infringement

WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW
  • Cast on and Bind off
  • Decreasing (plain or fancy)
  • Short Row Shaping
  • Ribbing (with ribber or hand manipulated) is optional
  • If not ribbing, an alternate cuff and hem finishing method
Why Upside Down?
One might say, "Why do this upside down?" IT'S EASIER! The sweater is knit all in one piece. You are able to knit patterns of fairisle, lace, plaiting, or tuck without the aggravation or hinderance of needles in the Hold position as you shape the raglan armhole.
THE ONE Trick to Success (Don't Skip This)
THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT STEP IN KNITTING
All of these patterns have been written for SPECIFIC GAUGES
The patterns are written for these gauges (not all sizes are available in all gauges):
  • 8sts/11 rows = 1" (32sts/44rows per 4"/10cm)
  • 4sts/6 rows = 1" (16sts/24rows per 4"/10cm)
  • 4.5sts/6.5 rows = 1" (18sts/26rows per 4"/10cm)
  • 5sts/7 rows = 1" (20sts/28rows per 4"/10cm)
IF YOU TRY AND KNIT THESE PATTERNS WITH A STITCH GAUGE OTHER THAN THE ABOVE ALL BETS ARE OFF AS TO THE SIZE YOU WILL HAVE WHEN THE SWEATER IS FINISHED. THE SIZING IS ONLY VALID WHEN YOU HAVE AN ACCURATE STITCH GAUGE AND KNOW EXACTLY WHAT TENSION TO USE ON THE SPECIFIC DYE LOT OF THE YARN YOU HAVE CHOSEN.
From Jodie I have found that it is best to make my swatch, tube it, steam it, etc., and then let it rest overnight. The next day, I check it to see if it is the same as it was before. Saves many headaches to know that one has a secure gauge. I always feel more confident my sweater will fit the size I'm trying to make, when I have an accurate and true stitch gauge.
From Sue I don't steam or wet block until the next day. Yes, it takes longer to establish gauge, but with natural fibers I find it more accurate to wait and let the swatch rest.
Don't skip making your gauge. And, remember, you must make a stitch gauge for every different dye lot of the same color yarn. Don't ever take for granted that you can always knit a certain brand of yarn at the same tension. The dye colors make the same yarns knit up differently.
If you have several different yarns you know you will be working on soon, take a morning out and make all your stitch gauges at one time. The next opportunity you have to knit, your gauge will be ready. TRICK: By changing the tension one or two dots tighter or looser, the same pattern will make a little smaller, or larger sweater. One full tension difference usually makes one complete size change.
Diagram VS written instructions
This pattern contains both diagram and written instructions for making all these raglans.
If you have not tried knitting from a diagram, you may find after you use it for awhile that it is a tremendous way to follow your pattern. You only need an occasional glance at your diagram to see what will be coming up next.
The patterns are read from the bottom to the top of the diagrams, except for the sleeves (which are knitted from the top of the sleeve to the wrist). That is why the diagrams are upside-down.
Allow your imagination to take over with these patterns
In addition to the classic sport pullover we all love, try a dressy look raglan. They are beautiful. Make it lacy, plain, dressy, sporty, short sleeve, long sleeve, crew neck, mock turtleneck, or the regular turtleneck.
Consider a Cardigan.

For both round and V, the front neckline is shaped at the same time the raglan shaping is worked.
The round front neckline is shaped from the band, using short Row Shaping to create 2 triangles on each side.
V neck shaping is created by knitting 2 separate triangles. These triangles are then attached to the neckband.
Although neither style is difficult to knit, it can be a bit confusing the first time through.
Please watch the videos carefully before starting to knit.
Want to skip the shaping (or knit a deeper or wider neckline)? Use cut 'n Sew
  • Do not knit the band according to the pattern
  • Knit 2 back pieces, starting with waste yarn and ravel cord.
  • Start the sleeves on waste yarn, but follow the pattern to join the body pieces as the sleeves are being knit
  • When the body pieces and sleeves are complete, use a cut-n-sew method to shape your neckline to any width and depth you like
  • Knit a separate neck band and attach it to your cut 'n sew opening by hand

The neckband is knit first and scrapped off in sections corresponding with the garment pieces (Back, Front, Sleeves)
Neckband options Plain or fancy, the neckband for a pullover needs to be stretchy, no tight cast on edge or stitch pattern without stretch.
For Babies and kids, from Jodie: "Because it is so hard to get the baby's head into a neckband that will fit nicely when on, it is recommended the neckline seam not be seamed. Close the opening by crocheting an edge around the seamline and fastening with either small buttons or velcro. If seaming, please rib very loosely and test the ribbing over the head before completing the sweater."
Make sure the neckband is large enough so it will stretch over the head

sections.title: SINGLE ROLLED EDGE (no ribber)
sections.bodyHtml:
This is the style used in the start-to-finish videos
  • No Ribber? This is a great casual finish
  • Fast Knitting
  • Be sure to use a VERY Stretchy Cast on
  1. Loosely cast on according to your pattern
  2. Knit 8-12 rows
  3. Scrap this neckband off in four sections.

sections.title: SINGLE RIBBED CREWNECK
sections.bodyHtml:
Note
If you don't have a ribber, hand knit, or hand manipulate ribbing for the neck band. Knit 1 plain row and scrap off. Mark the "right" or "wrong" side to help in re-hanging the neckband so the purl bumps of the plain row present on your preferred side
  • This is good for little children's sweaters as it has the least bulk under their chins.
  • Many people who have short necks look better with this type collar
  • It is great for those persons who do not like the feel of a lot of yarn up around their necks
  • It is cooler
  1. Using your ribber manual, cast-on the ribbing of your choice -1x1; 2x1; 2x2, etc. over the amount of needles required in your pattern for neckband. Rib for 12 rows.
  2. Transfer your ribber stitches up to the main bed.
  3. Knit one row across all these stitches with main garment yarn at main garment tension.
  4. Break yarn. Carriage is now on left.
  5. Scrap this neckband off in four sections.

sections.title: DOUBLE RIBBED CREWNECK
sections.bodyHtml:
• Rib 20 to 24 rows for children's sizes
  • 24 to 30 rows for adult sizes
  1. Transfer all ribber stitches up to the main bed
  2. Drop your ribber bed and remove the ribber comb and weights from the edge of your ribbing.
  3. Fold the bottom edge up and hang the ribbing edge on every other corresponding needle.
  4. Set the main bed carriage two full tensions looser than garment tension
  5. Knit one row across all stitches to enclose your neckband. This will reduce the doubled stitches from hanging the ribbed edge, down to a single stitch on 'each needle. We do this loosely so that it will slip over the head
  6. Break yarn.
  7. Scrap this piece off into four sections

sections.title: TURTLENECK CLOSE FITTING
sections.bodyHtml:
Use the same directions above for "Doubled Crewneck"
  • Rib desired number of rows - grading tensions on both the ribber carriage and the main carriage:
  • Upon completion, enclose the band, using directions from "Doubled Crewneck"
  • Pin the neckband together and try it over a head before going on to make sure it will fit. If a bit too snug, open your tension a little on your ribbing for the neckband.

sections.title: TURNING ROW OPTIONS
sections.bodyHtml:
When knitting a doubled band, a distinct turning row adds a professional touch. Here are some options: Loose turn row:
  1. Knit up to the turn row in the pattern.
  2. Put your tension up 4 full numbers looser and knit one row.
  3. Be careful to remember to change your tension back down to a tension tighter than garment tension for the backs side of this neckband.

Garter Bar turn edge:

This is a crisp, sharp, tailored edge.
  1. When you reach your turn row, use the garter bar and turn the band over
  2. Knit one row
  3. Remove on the garter bar again
  4. Rehang and turn band back to the purl side and continue knitting

Picot turn row Edge:

This is a feminine edge for ladies and children's garments.
  1. When you reach the turn row, transfer every other stitch to the adjoining needle.
  2. Leave the emptied needles in work position so they will knit.
  3. Knit 1 row
  4. Continue with the band instructions

The order of knitting:

  1. Right and left triangles for front neck shaping
  2. Neckband (with triangles attached)
  3. Neckband scrapped off in sections
  4. Back
  5. Front
  6. Sleeves

Alternate neckbands:

Mock Rib Band:
  1. After you have hung your neckband as instructed, transfer every other stitch to the adjoining needle.
  2. Push emptied needles back to out-of-work position.
  3. Turn the tension 2 full tension tighter than the garment tension.
  4. Knit both front and back of band.
  5. Hang and sew off.
This mock rib can be changed by emptying every 3rd or 4th stitch as well.
NOTE: Mock rib does not have enough stretch for the round neck raglan style.

Ribbed Band:
  • Hang your neckband as instructed.
  • Put your ribber bed up and transfer your stitches to the needle arrangement you desire (1x1, 1x2 etc).
  • Rib about 12 rows
  • Use the Easy Bind Off Method to bind the stitches

If you would like a neckband that crosses over at the front V, decrease your outside neckband stitches every other row. This requires only half as many decreases as written. It also requires half as many increases. When the edges are slip stitched together with the neckline it is very attractive, especially in the ribbing, loose turn row, or the garter bar turn row variation.

Please read this
Unlike the usual Knit it Now patterns, these patterns are written for SPECIFIC GAUGES.
Often knitters will substitute gauges for patterns:
  • Casting on more or fewer stitches and knitting more or fewer rows.
  • With other styles of knitting patterns, one can also use a ratioto adjust your knitting pattern to your gauge.
However these work-arounds can get complicated when shaping your knitting - especially armholes.
This is especially true with these top down raglan patterns.
The raglan armholes are shaped every other row. The angle of the shaping is set. so if you knit more or fewer rows, you are not only impacting the depth of the armhole, you are impacting the bust, chest size.
So when choosing yarn for these patterns, take care to match the gauge so your sweater fits both the armhole depth and the bust size.

DECIDING THE SIZE TO MAKE
The chest or bust measurements are really your most important guides. Check the measurements under the stitches of front and back on the diagrams to see how much allowance is in your particular size.
Armhole depth size.
To measure the depth:
  • Start a tape at the highest point of the shoulder at the base of the neck
  • Bring the tape over the shoulder point and down the outside of the arm to an imaginary line even with a pencil which is held between'the arm and the chest at the armhole.
  • This will give you the length of the armhole depth.
  • Check the measurement chart and decide which size comes nearer the measurements you have taken.
    Remember, a raglan armhole is usually 1" to 2" deeper than a normal set-in sleeve armhole. So, please take this into consideration when deciding which size you want to make. It will affect the length of the body of the sweater and the sleeves.
Custom Sizing
  • The sleeve length and wrist circumference can be adjusted using the tool in this course
  • The overall garment length can be adjusted by knitting more or fewer rows for the front and back between the armhole and hem.

sections.title: Critical tips for machine knitting accurate gauge swatches
sections.bodyHtml:
The whole point of a swatch is to accurately determine how many stitches and rows you are getting with YOUR yarn on YOUR machine. For accuracy, you don't measure a swatch from edge to edge, you measure in the center of the swatch.

  1. It's important to knit a swatch that is large enough to measure AT LEAST 4" square in the middle.
  2. To prevent errors, knit the same number of stitches and rows on every swatch you knit on a specific machine.
  3. Use contrasting color yarn of a similar weight to your garment weight to mark the center area of your swatch
  4. Permanently record your tension setting on your swatch (eyelets or tag)
  5. Let your swatch rest before measuring
  6. Dress your swatch as you will treat your finished knitting.
  7. Measure accurately - both flat and hanging
  8. Swatch for every stitch pattern you will be knitting

sections.title: Traditional Swatching
sections.bodyHtml:
• Machine knitters will often use these "rules" for establishing gauge
  • For a standard gauge machine, mark 40 sts and 60 rows in the middle of your swatch
  • For a mid-gauge machine, mark 30 sts and 40 rows
  • For a bulky/chunky machine, mark 20 sts and 30 rows
    • Armed with this information, you can adjust your tension to match the gauge used in these Upside Down Raglan patterns

The round neck knitting order:
  1. Knit the band
  2. Knit the back
  3. Knit the front
  4. Knit the sleeves and join front and back at the same time
  5. Seam the side seam and underarm
  6. Work in ends and final block
  7. Enjoy!

V-Neck order of knitting:
  1. Knit the front neck triangles
  2. Hang the triangles and knit the band
  3. Knit the back
  4. Knit the front
  5. Knit the sleeves and join front and back at the same time
  6. Seam the underarm and side seams
  7. Work in ends and final blocking
  8. Enjoy!
NOTE: This demo V-neck was a first run-through for me. Here are some thoughts about this experiment.
  • It's a kids size 4 with a fairly heavy yarn (Malabrigo Rios). For the smaller sizes, I'd choose a lighter weight yarn
  • According to the original pattern, the neckband is 1". At this gauge and at this size, I found the neckband to be too wide. I modified the pattern for the band to be smaller at the smaller sizes. You might want to check the row count of your band instructions and determine how wide you want your band
  • This Malbrigo yarn is "hand painted" you can clearly see the different dye lots when I switched balls. Normally when using this type of yarn you'd mix up the strands knitting a few rows of one end and a few rows of a different end. I was so focused on the construction of the V-neck that I didn't pay attention until the pieces were knit. Lesson learned: pay attention (or choose a different yarn for this type of knitting)

components.html:
The neckline is shaped AT THE SAME TIME as the raglan increases.
Each side is worked separately. When the neckline shaping is complete, the raglan increase continue.
  • The RAGLAN INCREASES are created just like the back raglan edges by pulling one needle into working position ON THE CARRIAGE SIDE.
    This creates an increase every other row on the raglan edge
  • Each NECKLINE INCREASE is worked with short rows OVER 2 ROWS. This means it takes 2 passes of the carriage to complete each NECKLINE INCREASE SEQUENCE.
    (The purpose of this is to increase neatly with automatic wraps and prevent holes between the neckline edge and the neckband)
These increase are worked AT THE SAME TIME

Neckline Increase Sequence (left side of needlebed):
  1. Carriage set to hold
  2. Carriage on the LEFT
  3. On the carriage side: Put 2 needles with stitches into working position
    ~and~ put ONE EMPTY NEEDLE into working position
    This increases 1 raglan stitch on the left and 1 neckline stitch (plus a stitch for wrapping) on the right
  4. Knit to the RIGHT
  5. On the carriage side (right): Pull 1 needle to hold position for automatic wrap
    This prevents a hole
  6. Knit to the LEFT (2 needles in work)
This completes the NECKLINE INCREASE SEQUENCE for the left side. You will repeat this as instructed in the pattern.
Each time, you will be putting and empty needle into work on the left and increasing needles as directed on the right.

Steps 3 and 4 complete increases for BOTH the neck and raglan Edge.
Steps 5 and 6 create the wrap to prevent holes.
When the left side is complete, repeat the shaping, reversing the instructions
Neckline Increase Sequence (right side of needlebed):
  1. Carriage set to hold
  2. Carriage on the RIGHT
  3. On the carriage side: Put 2 needles with stitches into working position
    ~and~ put ONE EMPTY NEEDLE into working position
  4. Knit to the LEFT
  5. On the carriage side (left): Pull on needle to hold position for automatic wrap
  6. Knit to the RIGHT
This completes the NECKLINE INCREASE SEQUENCE for the right side

To knit the Upside Down V-Neck as a cardigan, you will knit the neckband last. Follow the steps below.
NOTE:We HIGHLY recommend that you knit the pullover version before attempting to knit a v-neck cardigan. For success, take time to knit the practice V-Neck V sweater first

sections.title: Knit the front triangles
sections.bodyHtml: Follow the pattern instructions and knit the front triangles.  Scrap off as instructed

sections.title: Start Knitting
sections.bodyHtml:
Unlike the pullover version, the body pieces will not be picked up from the band.
The order of knitting is the same as the pullover version: back, front 1, front 2, sleeve 1, sleeve 2.
When the body pieces are complete (joining the back and front as the sleeves are knit, the neck band is knitted last.
Order of Knitting (the same as the pullover version):
  1. Back: Cast on (waste yarn or e-wrap) the back stitches as instructed. Knit the back
  2. Front 1: Pick up triangle edge as instructed and knit the front over 1/2 the stitches indicated in the pattern
  3. Front 2: Pick up the triangle edge as instructed and knit the remaining front
  4. Sleeves: Cast on (waste yarn or e-wrap) the sleeve stitches as instructed. Knit the sleeve, joining the associated back and front armhole
  5. Repeat for the second sleeve

sections.title: Band Options
sections.bodyHtml:
Once the body of the sweater is finished, there are many options for finishing the neckband and button/buttonhole bands.
  1. By hand: pick up the entire neck and cardigan opening and knit in the stitch pattern of your choice
  2. By machine:
    • Pick up the back neck and sleeve stitches and knit a band as desired (remember to add seaming stitches)
    • Pick up each front edge separately
    • As you pick up the front edge, add additional stitches at the point of the V to "turn the corner"
    • Seam the bands

From Jodie:
In most of my knitting, I prefer to make the back section first. It usually has the least shaping; therefore, it is the easiest.
When it is completed:
  • Take it to the blocking board. Using the blocking measurements from your diagram (be sure to get the right measurements from the page for the size you are knitting), pin it out to see if it is working out correctly.
  • If the measurements are correct, go ahead and steam it.
  • If the measurements are incorrect, try to see what your problem might be. Check your stitch gauge again or your machine tension
    Maybe, you will have to rip it out; but, at least it is only the back and the yarn will still be usable since no steam has been put to it as yet.
  • Continue to check and block each piece as it comes from the machine. The stitches to be picked up will be easier to find, and the garment will need only a steam touch-up along the seams when you are finished weaving it together.
Blocking is one of the most important steps in turning out a great looking garment.
Use enough steam to really set the stitches. I use a sole plate over my iron for steaming.
DO NOT BLOCK THE RIBBING. It will lose it's elasticity.
Do insert a wooden spoon handle, or dowel, into the doubled bands of Mock Ribbing, or other doubled bands, and gently tug the stitches into place. Also, on the edge of regular ribbing, I take a double-eye needle, run it through the caston edge, and pull on these stitches. It takes the curling out of the edge and sets these stitches. Looks a great deal better.
After the sweater is knitted and blocked
  • Weave the neckband together with a bar-to-bar stitch - maintaining the established ribbed pattern.
  • Using the yarn at the top of each sleeve's raglan slant, weave the last loop into the neckband, tie off and hide yarn in collar.
  • Weave the sweater together with the same bar-to-bar stitch, beginning at the bottom edge of body and moving toward the underarm.
  • Then weave the sleeve in the same fashion, starting at cuff and moving toward the underarm.
  • If using a lace or fairisle pattern, be sure to match up your design.
  • At all times one should make the decreases match when sewing a garment together.
  • Secure and tie off. Slip ends into the seams.

sections.title: Mock Ribbing
sections.bodyHtml:
There is a mock rib edge for the end of the bottoms and cuffs that is very nice. And it is FAST!
NOTE: Mock Ribbing is not suitable for the round neckband. It does not have enough stretch. If you use Mock Ribbing for the hem and cuffs, choose a different method for the neckband.
  1. After the last row of the bottom and sleeve of the sweater, just transfer every other stitch to the adjoining needle. (If you are knitting on a standard machine, the lace carriage can make quick work of this).
  2. Turn tension two full tensions tighter than main garment tension.
  3. On your first row of this rib, put in a marker row of different colored crochet cotton, or ravel cord, with your garment yarn so you can see where to hang these stitches later.
  4. Knit twice the number of rows you want for your ribbing on every other needle
  5. When desired rows are knit, hang stitches on corresponding needles and loosely sew off with a double-eye needle threaded with garment yarn.

sections.title: Kitchener Join
sections.bodyHtml:
Create a ribbing cast on, knit your ribbing, then seam it to the body of your upside down sweater.
  • Using your ribber, make the ribbing for the neck, two bottoms, and two sleeve cuffs all at one time -scrapping each one off with about 8 rows of scrap yarn.
  • When knitting your sweater pieces,scrap off the end of each piece with about 8 rows of scrap yarn (bottoms and sleeves).
  • Before blocking, Kitchener the ribbed pieces to the sweater pieces. It takes a little extra time, but the finished sweater is worth it!

From Jodie:
This is an "upside-down" sweater.
If you are knitting in pattern and the stitch pattern has a definite top and bottom, you must turn your pattern card upside down (or use a pattern variation on an electronic machine).

STITCH PATTERN PLACEMENT
Some liberties of one or two stitches, or rows, have been taken with these diagrams in order to accommodate automatic pattern cards.
These sweaters have been designed to use the 12-wide automatic punch card patterns. On some,the designs will come out with an even number of full repeats.
Two seaming stitches have been allowed in all patterns. On some sizes, the dimensions turn out with half of a repeat, plus the two seaming stitches. When these are sewn together,the seam will form another perfect stitch pattern repeat.
Patterning Tips:
  • Remember, ALWAYS KEEP THE FIRST AND LAST STITCHES ON ALL PIECES MADE WITH TWO COLOR WORK IN MAIN GARMENT COLOR. If the automatic pattern selector moves the end needles out for color work, move them by hand back to the working position before knitting across that row.
  • Some sizes work out alright for the 24 wide automatic punch card machines. You must divide the chest, or bust,measurements on your diagram by 24. Don't forget to add the two seaming stitches on each piece. If there is no way of this working out well, try centering a design and using only a few of the repeats. Just push the needles programmed that will not make a complete pattern, back to working position by hand, before you knit across.
  • Many 24 wide pattern cards are only 12 wide patterns -twice on a card. They will work out just fine.
  • Give it some thought and it is not really very hard to figure out how to use many of the beautiful stitch patterns available.
No matter what stitch pattern you choose, you MUST MATCH the pattern gauge to obtain the correct size.
